title: Units & Values
summary: CSS values use units to describe sizes, colors, and other visual choices.

subtopics.title: Pixels
subtopics.explanation: `px` is a CSS pixel, a fixed layout unit that browsers map to the display. It is like using a ruler with a chosen mark size. It can work for fine borders, but fixed text sizes may not adapt as well to user preferences. For example, use rem for text so the page follows a user-adjusted root size.

subtopics.title: Root text size
subtopics.explanation: `rem` is based on the root element’s text size. It is like measuring from a shared ruler for the whole page. Using rem for typography and spacing can make consistent scaling easier when the root size changes. For example, use a percentage when a child should track its containing panel.

subtopics.title: Percentages
subtopics.explanation: `%` depends on another size, often the containing block’s dimension. It is like measuring a portion of a parent container. The result changes when that parent changes, so check the layout at different widths and understand which parent controls the percentage. For example, a fixed border thickness can use a pixel value while the card width stays flexible.

subtopics.title: Viewport units
subtopics.explanation: `vw` and `vh` relate to the viewport width and height. They can create responsive sizing, but full viewport height has edge cases on mobile browser chrome. It is like measuring against the visible window. Prefer modern small or dynamic viewport units when the browser support target allows them. For example, viewport units can size a hero but should not make body text unreadably small.

subtopics.title: Choose a relationship
subtopics.explanation: Choose units based on the relationship you want. Text may need to scale with user settings; a border may need a steady thickness; a panel may follow its parent width. It is like picking the right ruler for a task. Avoid choosing units by habit without checking the result. For example, test the layout at high zoom and narrow widths after changing a unit.

foundations.overview: CSS units describe lengths and sizes. Some are fixed relative to a CSS pixel; others scale with text, a parent, or the viewport. Think of them as different rulers for different jobs. Choose a unit based on what should control the size, then test zoom and narrow screens so the layout remains usable.
foundations.whyItMatters: The unit determines which context controls a size. Choosing that relationship deliberately makes a layout more adaptable to text preferences, container changes, and different screens.
foundations.browserPerspective: When the browser computes styles, it resolves every relative unit to absolute pixels using the relevant reference (root size for rem, element size for em, parent size for %, viewport size for vw/vh) before layout and paint.
foundations.realWorldUsage: rem for typography and spacing, em for component-internal padding, % for fluid widths, vh for full-height sections, and ch for readable text columns are the everyday combinations in production design systems.
foundations.businessImpact: Layouts that scale with user settings and screen sizes reach more users (including those who increase font size for readability), improving accessibility compliance and engagement.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A consistent unit strategy (e.g. rem-based spacing scale) reduces magic numbers and makes responsive behavior predictable and easy to adjust globally.
foundations.performanceImpact: Units themselves don't affect performance meaningfully, but viewport units that change on scroll (mobile vh) can cause layout shifts; choosing stable units avoids jank.
commonUseCases: rem for font sizes and a global spacing scale
% and max-width for fluid, capped containers
vh for full-screen sections and vw for fluid hero text
ch to constrain readable line length

commonMisconceptions.myth: px and rem are interchangeable for font sizes.
commonMisconceptions.reality: px ignores the user's browser font-size setting; rem scales with it, which matters for accessibility.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Percentage vertical padding is relative to height.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Percentage padding and margin are always relative to the parent's WIDTH, even top/bottom values.

commonMisconceptions.myth: line-height should use em or px for precision.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unitless line-height is preferred because it inherits as a ratio, so each element computes the correct height for its own font size.
It depends on the root font size, which users or styles can change.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Viewport units are a complete responsive strategy.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They do not replace content-aware breakpoints, flexible sizing, or accessibility checks.

visualExplorer.title: How units resolve
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how the browser turns each relative unit into pixels using its reference value.

steps.title: px (absolute)
steps.description: A fixed size. 16px is always 16px regardless of context — used for borders and fine details.

steps.title: rem (root-relative)
steps.description: Multiplied by the root font size. With root 16px, 1.5rem resolves to 24px and scales globally if the root changes.

steps.title: em (element-relative)
steps.description: Multiplied by the element's own font size; compounds when nested, so 1.2em inside 1.2em grows quickly.

steps.title: % (parent-relative)
steps.description: A fraction of the parent's dimension; width: 50% is half the parent, and % padding references the parent's width.

steps.title: vw / vh (viewport-relative)
steps.description: 1% of the viewport width or height; 100vh fills the screen and 5vw scales text with window width.

codeLab.title: Build an accessible, fluid card
codeLab.instructions: Style .card to be fluid but capped: use a percentage width with a rem-based max-width, rem padding, unitless line-height, and a ch-based max-width on the text so lines stay readable. Avoid px for font size and spacing. Hints below.

codeLab.expectedOutput: A centered card that shrinks on narrow screens, never exceeds 30rem wide, and keeps text at a readable measure.

keyTakeaways: `px` is a CSS pixel, a fixed layout unit that browsers map to the display.
`rem` is based on the root element’s text size.
`%` depends on another size, often the containing block’s dimension.
`vw` and `vh` relate to the viewport width and height.
Choose units based on the relationship you want.
